top_cluster.headline: Two House Republicans face separate misconduct scandals — Rep. Chuck Edwards recommended for censure over harassment of young female staffers, and Rep. Max Miller refusing to withdraw from reelection despite domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife — as Democrats push for resignations or expulsion and the GOP confronts ballot and accountability deadlines.
top_cluster.left_framing: Center-left outlets (NPR, PBS) treat both cases as institutional accountability failures, emphasizing bipartisan ethics findings, the moral weight of a senator breaking with his own former son-in-law over abuse allegations, and the GOP's discomfort in policing its own members ahead of a hard ballot deadline.
top_cluster.center_framing: Center outlets (The Hill, Axios) frame both stories through a process and horse-race lens — ballot-deadline logistics, succession speculation (Renacci), and internal Democratic strategizing over whether to force an expulsion vote — rather than dwelling on the substance or severity of the allegations themselves.
top_cluster.right_framing: Right-leaning coverage in this set (Fox News) addresses the Edwards ethics finding fairly directly and factually, including his denial, but no outlet on the right covers the Max Miller domestic abuse story at all — right-of-center attention here is concentrated instead on unrelated stories (denaturalization, judicial impeachment threats, Iran, Pentagon strikes).
top_cluster.left_omissions: Left-leaning coverage does not surface the insider detail (reported by Axios, a center outlet) that Trump privately told Miller his candidacy was in trouble while staying publicly silent, nor does it engage with Edwards' attorneys' counter-argument that the ethics recommendation overreaches.
top_cluster.right_omissions: Right-leaning outlets in this set almost entirely omit the Max Miller domestic abuse story — no Fox News or Breitbart piece addresses it, despite it being one of the more heavily covered GOP accountability stories across NPR, PBS, The Hill, and Axios — leaving a notable coverage gap on a sitting Republican member's alleged domestic abuse.

blindspot_narrative: Right-leaning outlets are systematically avoiding stories that reflect poorly on their own coalition in ways harder to spin than routine partisan attacks: Miller's domestic abuse allegations, federal worker relocation conditions, and Iran-linked infrastructure cyberattacks that complicate a deterrence narrative. Left-leaning outlets are avoiding stories showing Democratic leadership faltering or fracturing internally, most notably Schumer's shutdown concession, while ceding the Democratic-socialist-wing fight (Mamdani, Hong, Cori Bush) to right-only framing rather than contesting it directly. Both patterns point to the same underlying behavior: each side covers intra-institutional accountability stories only when the institution being scrutinized belongs to the other camp.
